function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete “what‑to‑do” guide** that walks through every item in your list – from pulling the repo locally up to committing the new artefacts back to GitHub.  
Because I don’t have live SSH access inside this chat window, I’ll walk you through what *you* would normally run on your machine.  

---

## 1️⃣  Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you’re authenticated with SSH keys
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"

# Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you already cloned the repo somewhere else, jump straight to Step 2.

---

## 2️⃣  Analyse the Project Structure

Open the folder and take note of the key items:

| File / Folder | Typical Purpose |
|---------------|----------------|
| `package.json` | Defines scripts (`start`, `test`) and deps |
| `.dockerignore` | Optional – usually contains `node_modules`, logs, etc. |
| `src/index.js` (or similar) | Entry point of the NodeJS app |
| `README.md` | Documentation |

If anything looks different, feel free to tweak the templates below.

### 2.1 ‑ Dockerfile

Create a lightweight Alpine‑based image that installs production deps only.

```dockerfile
# ────────────────────── Dockerfile ──────────────────────────── #
# Build Stage -----------------------------------------------------#
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder          # <-- choose latest LTS
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy lockfile(s) first to leverage cached layers
COPY package*.json ./

# Install prod deps only
RUN npm ci --omit dev && rm -rf ~/.npm/_cacache/*

# Copy source after deps to avoid rebuild on change
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
ENV PORT=${PORT:-3000}
EXPOSE ${PORT}

# Default CMD
ENTRYPOINT [ "node", "src/index.js" ]
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ #
```

> Save this as `./Dockerfile`.  
> Adjust the `ENTRYPOINT` line if your start script lives elsewhere (e.g. `server.js`).  
> You may also wish to pin the exact Node version (`node:20-alpine`) or switch to `slim`.

### 2.2 ‑ Kubernetes YAML

A single manifest containing both Deployment and Service makes life easier.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3                     # scale as needed
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:<TAG>
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000     # matches EXPOSE in Dockerfile
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer                # Change to ClusterIP / NodePort if preferred
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                        # External port exposed by GCP/AWS/etc.
    targetPort: 3000                # Container port
```

Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` and `<TAG>` with whatever registry/tag strategy you adopt (e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:v1.0.0`).

### 2.3 ‑ GitHub Actions Workflow

Add a CI pipeline that builds the Docker image, runs tests, and optionally publishes the image.

Create `/.github/workflows/build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Test

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-test-publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write           # Needed if publishing to GHCR
      id-token: write           # Required for OIDC auth

    services:
      postgres:                  # Example of adding a DB service if required
        image: postgres:15
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: test_user
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
          POSTGRES_DB: test_db
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5

    steps:
    - name: Checkout Code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version-file: '.nvmrc'   # or specify explicit version

    - name: Cache NPM modules
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.npm
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-npm-

    - name: Install Dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run Tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Login to GitHub Packages
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build Docker Image
      run: |
        IMAGE_NAME="ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}:${{ github.sha }}"
        echo "$IMAGE_NAME"
        docker buildx bake \
          --set *.platform=linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
          --push \
          --output=image="$IMAGE_NAME" \
          ./docker-bake.hcl || true

    - name: Push Docker Image
      run: |
        IMAGE_TAG="${{ github.ref_name }}"       # e.g. main -> latest
        docker tag $(docker images -q ghcr.io/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY:$SHA) ghcr.io/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY:${IMAGE_TAG}
        docker push ghcr.io/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY:${IMAGE_TAG}
```

#### Notes

* Replace the `services:` section with any database or cache your app needs during testing. Remove it if unnecessary.
* The `buildx bake` block assumes you’ve added a `docker-bake.hcl` describing multi‑arch builds. If you prefer plain `docker build`, replace that part with:

  ```yaml
  - name: Build Docker Image
    run: |
      IMAGE="ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}:${{ github.sha }}"
      docker build -t $IMAGE .
      docker push $IMAGE
  ```

* Ensure you store the resulting image under a public/private registry accessible to your cluster.

---

## 3️⃣  Stage All New Files

From within the repo’s root:

```bash
git add Dockerfile
git add k8s.yaml               # rename if you saved differently
git add .github/workflows/*.yml
```

(Use `git status` to double‑check.)

---

## 4️⃣  Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "CI/CD: Added Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow."
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, GitHub Actions will trigger immediately (if you set `workflow_dispatch` or a push event). Verify the job succeeded in the **Actions** tab.

---

## 🎉 What Happens Next?

1. **Container Registry:** Your image lands at `ghcr.io/<org>/<repo>:<sha>`.  
2. **Deployments:** Apply the K8s manifest (`kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml`) whenever you release a new tag or merge to `main`.  
3. **Scaling & Observability:** With the Service marked `LoadBalancer`, cloud providers auto‑allocate an IP. Monitor traffic, health checks, and autoscaling rules per your infra policy.

Feel free to tweak any defaults—especially replica counts, resource limits, or environment variables—to suit your operational requirements. Happy coding!
